1.overview: Research is a systematic, critical and purposeful process of asking questions, examining evidence and building or refining knowledge. The opening course material uses discussion to explore what research is and what a research degree asks of a learner. It is not merely attending classes or collecting facts: the learner must learn to frame questions, tolerate uncertainty, reason independently and communicate what the evidence supports.
sections: 1. What research involves
A question or problem gives research direction.
The researcher reviews what is already known before deciding what remains unclear.
A method is selected to gather or analyse evidence; the method should fit the question.
Results must be interpreted carefully and communicated so others can evaluate the reasoning.
Example: Instead of asking “Is this sensor good?”, define a measurable question such as whether its readings agree with a reference instrument across a specified range.
2. Research-based degrees
Research degrees place substantial weight on independent inquiry and sustained investigation.
Critical thinking means assessing claims and assumptions rather than accepting them automatically.
Analytical ability includes breaking a complex problem into parts, comparing evidence and drawing reasoned conclusions.
Research questions and approaches can evolve as evidence is discovered.
Contrast: coursework mainly assesses learning of an established body of material; a research project also asks the learner to investigate a question that is not fully answered in advance.
3. Working with an advisor and research community
Agree on expectations, milestones, communication frequency and feedback process.
Bring specific questions and evidence to meetings; record decisions and next actions.
Use feedback to improve the work, while retaining responsibility for the research.
Research is independent work, but not isolated work: discussion can expose blind spots.
A useful meeting note records the issue, what was tried, what the evidence showed and the next experiment or reading task.
4. Failure, iteration and small steps
Research outcomes are not guaranteed. An unexpected or negative result can still be informative when the experiment and analysis are sound.
Use a failed attempt to revisit assumptions, check the method and design a more informative next test.
Progress is often cumulative: small experiments and careful observations can support a larger contribution over time.
Example: If a sensor does not behave as expected, verify wiring and calibration, record the conditions, and test one plausible cause at a time.
5. Industry problem-solving and fundamental science
Engineering work often asks how to improve a product, compare batches, reduce parts or select a suitable material under practical constraints.
Scientific inquiry asks why a property exists, what mechanism produces it and what limits may apply.
Connecting practical engineering questions with fundamental science helps researchers explain observations and create better solutions.
Study prompt: classify a question as primarily practical engineering, fundamental science, or a combination.
key: Research is inquiry, not just information collection.
Critical thinking and analytical ability are central research skills.
A research path is open-ended: evidence may change the next question.
Clear advisor communication prevents avoidable ambiguity.
Failure, iteration and small steps
Industry problem-solving and fundamental science

Why does research require critical thinking?

2.overview: A literature survey establishes the context for a research question. It helps the researcher understand existing explanations and methods, find points of agreement or disagreement, identify gaps and avoid repeating work without justification. Week 2 also includes scholarly search tools, writing up, reference-management/bibliography tools and experimental skills.
sections: 1. Plan a literature search
Turn the broad topic into keywords and related terms.
Combine search terms deliberately; keep a record of queries and filters.
Use inclusion/exclusion criteria so the selection is not arbitrary.
Read titles and abstracts for screening, then inspect methods and results in relevant papers.
Example: For low-cost air-quality sensing, search related phrases such as low-cost sensor, calibration, particulate/gas measurement and field validation, then narrow by date or application.
2. Web of Science and Scopus
These are scholarly indexing and citation-search databases.
Search by topic, author, title, affiliation or publication details where supported.
Citation links can help follow how a paper was used by later work.
Database coverage differs; one database search should not be assumed to include every relevant publication.
Keep a search log with database, search string, date, filters and number of results. This makes the survey more transparent and repeatable.
3. Read and synthesise, do not merely list
For each source, note the question, method, evidence, main result and limitation.
Group papers by themes or approaches rather than writing one disconnected paragraph per paper.
Compare findings and explain why they differ where possible.
Use the synthesis to justify a research gap or a more precise question.
A literature matrix with columns for citation, objective, method, sample/data, findings, limitations and relevance makes comparisons easier.
4. Writing up and references
Cite the source of borrowed ideas, data, figures and exact wording.
Keep bibliographic details when you first save a paper.
Use a consistent citation style and verify generated reference entries.
A bibliography/reference list helps readers locate and check the sources.
Never rely on memory for page numbers, author spellings or publication years; verify these from the original source.
5. Experimental skills
Before running an experiment, define the objective, variables, equipment and recording procedure.
Check instrument range, calibration, units and safe operating limits.
Record unexpected observations rather than deleting them.
Follow the relevant laboratory safety instructions and risk controls.
A repeatable experiment requires enough procedural detail that another person can understand what was done and under what conditions.
6. Build a search strategy
Translate the research question into important concepts and synonyms before searching.
Use keyword searching to discover relevant work, then follow references backwards to locate earlier contributions and forward citations to see later work.
Record databases, keywords, date limits and screening decisions so the search can be repeated.
Example: Start with a device name and its alternate technical term, then search cited references from a relevant review.
7. Judge sources and preserve traceability
Primary sources such as original journal articles, research reports and conference proceedings report work directly; reviews and compilations synthesize existing work.
An open-access label means readers can access the article freely; it does not by itself guarantee or disprove quality.
DOIs are designed to identify digital scholarly objects; capture complete bibliographic details and cite the sources actually used.
Quick check: ask whether a source is relevant, credible, traceable, sufficiently complete and appropriate for the claim.
key: A literature survey is critical synthesis, not just a list of summaries.
Scopus and Web of Science are discovery/indexing tools; coverage may differ.
Record search strategy and bibliographic metadata.
Connect the gap in prior work to the research question.
Plan experiments with safety, measurement quality and repeatability in mind.
Build a search strategy
Judge sources and preserve traceability
check: What is the difference between summarising and synthesising papers?
Why keep a search log?
What should a literature matrix record?

3.overview: Data analysis turns observations into evidence that can be interpreted. Modelling represents a system or relationship in a simplified form. Good practice keeps raw observations, processing steps, assumptions, model outputs and conclusions distinguishable. The textbook also includes laboratory safety in this week.
sections: 1. Understand the data before analysis
Check units, missing values, duplicates, impossible values and measurement conditions.
Use tables and plots to inspect distributions, trends, outliers and relationships.
Distinguish a data-quality problem from a genuine unusual observation.
Document cleaning and transformations so the path from raw data to result is traceable.
Example: A temperature reading far outside the sensor range should be investigated as a possible sensor or logging error, not silently deleted.
2. Descriptive and inferential reasoning
Descriptive analysis summarises the observed data.
Inferential reasoning uses data to estimate or test claims about a broader process or population.
A relationship between two variables does not by itself establish causation.
Report uncertainty and sample limitations where they affect interpretation.
When comparing two conditions, state what was measured, how many observations were taken and whether the conditions were comparable.
3. Models and assumptions
A model simplifies reality to answer a specific question.
Identify inputs, outputs, parameters and assumptions before interpreting its results.
Fit or predictive performance should be checked using suitable evidence.
Avoid extrapolating far beyond the range or setting for which the model was evaluated.
A linear model may be useful over a limited range but can mislead if the underlying relationship changes outside that range.
4. Communicating results responsibly
Use a plot that matches the question and label axes with units.
Separate results from interpretation.
Report relevant limitations, unexpected findings and uncertainty.
Do not alter data to force a preferred conclusion.
A good result statement tells the reader what changed, by how much if known, and under which conditions.
5. Estimation, error and signal behaviour
An estimate is calculated from observations; its uncertainty depends on the data, measurement process and assumptions.
Standard deviation describes spread and is often used to describe uncertainty in repeated measurements or estimates, depending on context.
Do not treat faulty sensor readings as valid observations merely because a model can be fitted to them; identify and document instrument failures.
Example: A sensor that suddenly reports an implausible temperature needs inspection before its data are used to support a conclusion.
6. Linear and nonlinear models
A linear approximation is often local: a Taylor-series approximation depends on the chosen nominal operating point.
Nonlinear terms are not generally handled by simply deleting them without considering the approximation and its validity range.
Model quality should be assessed against the question, data quality, assumptions and residual error—not by assuming one model family is always better.
Study prompt: explain why a linearized model may be useful near one operating point but less reliable far away.
key: Inspect data quality before analysis.
Correlation alone does not prove causation.
A model is only as useful as its assumptions and validation.
Preserve traceability from raw data to final conclusion.
Laboratory safety and reliable measurement are part of sound research.
Estimation, error and signal behaviour
Linear and nonlinear models
check: Why should raw data be preserved?
What is an assumption in a model?

4.overview: Technical presentations and technical writing communicate a research argument. The reader or audience should be able to identify the problem, understand the method, evaluate the evidence and follow the conclusion. Structure and clarity are more important than decorative effects.
sections: 1. Build the argument before the slides
Define the audience and the single purpose of the presentation.
Introduce the problem and why it matters.
Explain the method at the level needed to interpret the results.
Present evidence before the conclusion and acknowledge important limitations.
A useful flow is context → problem/question → approach → evidence/results → interpretation → conclusion/next steps.
2. Slides and visuals
One slide should have one main message.
Use readable labels, consistent units and legends.
Choose a chart type that matches the comparison or trend.
Avoid dense paragraphs, unexplained abbreviations and decorative animation that distracts from evidence.
If a figure needs explanation, state the main takeaway in the slide title or a short caption.
3. Technical writing
Use precise words and define specialised terms when first introduced.
Organise sections so each paragraph advances one point.
Support factual claims with evidence and citations.
Distinguish what was measured from what is inferred.
Revise for accuracy, clarity, concision and consistency.
A strong paragraph often makes a claim, gives supporting evidence, explains its significance and connects to the next point.
4. Prepare for questions
Know why the method was chosen and what alternatives exist.
Be ready to explain assumptions, uncertainty and limitations.
If you do not know an answer, state the boundary of what the evidence supports.
A careful, evidence-based answer is stronger than a confident guess.
5. Use visuals as evidence
Choose a table when readers need to look up exact values; choose a graph when the main purpose is to show a trend, relationship or comparison.
Magnification and resolution are different: a larger image does not necessarily reveal more detail.
An image should show the level of detail required by the discussion, and a scale bar is important when size or dimensions matter.
Example: Use a graph to compare temperature over time, but a table when the reader must retrieve exact measured values.
6. Organize the reader’s journey
Chronological structure follows time; spatial structure follows physical arrangement; a variable-based structure follows changes in a chosen quantity.
Sentences should be concise and references such as “this” or “these” should clearly point to one antecedent.
Technical writing also includes safe practice: electricity hazards are not limited to voltage alone.
Self-check: for each paragraph, ask what the reader should learn and how it connects to the next paragraph.
key: Structure the research story logically.
Visuals should clarify evidence, not decorate the slide.
Technical writing prioritises precision, clarity and traceability.
Separate evidence, interpretation and limitation.
Use visuals as evidence
Organize the reader’s journey

5.overview: Week 5 brings creativity in research together with research ethics. Creativity involves exploring alternatives, reframing problems and questioning familiar assumptions. Functional fixedness is one barrier: a person may see an object or method only in its familiar role. Creativity must operate alongside honesty, fairness and responsibility.
sections: 1. Creativity as a process
Creativity is not only a fixed inborn talent; practice can improve how ideas are generated and evaluated.
Reframing a problem can reveal solutions hidden by the original wording.
Combining ideas from different contexts can suggest new approaches.
Idea generation and evidence-based evaluation are related but distinct stages.
Try asking: What assumption am I making? Can I define the problem another way? What would happen if a constraint changed?
2. Functional fixedness
Functional fixedness means seeing an object mainly in its conventional use.
It can limit the ability to imagine alternative uses or solutions.
Changing the representation of a problem can help break the constraint.
Do not confuse a familiar solution with the only possible solution.
Example: A container may be seen only as storage, even when its shape could help solve a different practical problem.
3. Ethics in research
Report methods and findings honestly.
Do not fabricate or falsify observations.
Give appropriate credit and avoid plagiarism.
Respect people, animals, privacy, safety and applicable approvals where relevant.
Disclose conflicts or limitations that could affect interpretation.
A result that contradicts the hypothesis is still a result; it should be investigated and reported honestly.
4. Creativity with integrity
Novelty does not justify misrepresenting evidence.
A clever idea should still be tested and evaluated.
Ethical constraints protect participants, colleagues, the public and the credibility of research.
When facing an ethical dilemma, identify stakeholders, potential harms, duties and relevant policies before acting.
5. Intelligence, stress and creative work
Sternberg’s practical intelligence concerns adapting to and managing real-world environments; creativity also involves generating new approaches.
Moderate, manageable positive stress (often called eustress) can support engagement, while excessive distress can interfere with performance.
Reading beyond one narrow topic can give a researcher more concepts and analogies to combine when solving a problem.
Example: A method from another field may inspire a new experiment, but its suitability must still be tested.
6. Ethical collaboration and professional contribution
Collaborators should understand and agree to authorship and publication plans; shared work does not justify publishing a joint result without appropriate agreement.
Professional research is judged by meaningful contributions, competence and scrutiny by peers—not simply local visibility.
Researchers should be aware of the literature and identify where their work can contribute rather than working in isolation from prior results.
Study prompt: explain why novelty, acknowledgement, author agreement and evidence quality all matter to research integrity.
key: Functional fixedness restricts alternative uses or framings.
Creative thinking can be developed through practice.
Research ethics includes honesty, proper attribution and responsible treatment of evidence.
Unexpected or negative results must not be hidden merely because they are inconvenient.
Intelligence, stress and creative work
Ethical collaboration and professional contribution

6.overview: Intellectual property (IP) concerns rights associated with creations of the mind. The supplied textbook dedicates two parts to IP, and the assignment screenshots include questions on IP rights and infringement. In revision, identify the kind of creation, the relevant right, who holds it, what use is proposed and which conditions or exceptions apply.
sections: 1. Identify the IP category
Different forms of IP protect different subject matter.
Inventions, original expressive works, brand identifiers and confidential know-how are not interchangeable categories.
The relevant protection, duration and conditions depend on the category and jurisdiction.
Do not assume that one form of registration protects every aspect of a product.
For a device, a technical invention, its software, its product name and its confidential manufacturing process may raise different IP questions.
2. Ownership, permission and infringement
Ownership and permission to use are different questions.
Attribution alone does not necessarily grant permission for every reuse.
Check licences, contracts, institutional policies and applicable law.
Infringement analysis depends on the protected right, the act performed and relevant limitations or exceptions.
Before reusing a figure, code, dataset or design, record its source and verify the terms that govern reuse.
3. IP in research and innovation
Discuss ownership and contribution expectations early in collaborative work.
Keep appropriate records of creation and development.
Consider disclosure timing before public release when IP protection may be relevant.
Respect third-party rights while sharing research responsibly.
For course-specific legal details, prioritise the wording and examples in the uploaded IP lectures and assignments; this summary is an orientation, not legal advice.
3. Match the IP right to the creation
Copyright protects qualifying expression such as written, artistic and other creative works; it does not grant ownership of every underlying idea.
Patents concern qualifying inventions and are granted under legal requirements; a patent is not the same thing as a trade mark.
Trade marks distinguish the commercial source of goods or services; passing off can protect goodwill against misrepresentation even where a mark is unregistered.
Example: a logo, an invention process and a written article raise different IP questions and should not be treated as the same right.
4. Rights, limits and international context
IP rights can allow exclusion of certain uses, commercial exploitation and legal action against infringement, subject to the applicable law.
In India, a patent generally lasts 20 years from the filing date, subject to statutory conditions and maintenance requirements.
TRIPS stands for Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights; it is an international agreement related to IP standards in trade.
Self-check: identify the creation, the relevant right, the owner, the duration/conditions and the use that may infringe.
key: Different IP categories protect different subject matter.
Attribution and permission are not identical.
Ownership, licences, contracts and exceptions may all matter.
The exact answer depends on the right and the facts.
Match the IP right to the creation
Rights, limits and international context

7.overview: Design of Experiments (DOE) is a systematic way to plan experiments so the effects of factors on measured responses can be studied. Rather than changing conditions casually, the researcher chooses combinations and procedures that support interpretable comparisons. The textbook contains five DOE parts.
sections: 1. Core terms
A factor is an input or condition deliberately varied or studied.
A level is a chosen setting of a factor.
A response is the measured outcome used to assess the experiment.
A treatment is a particular condition or combination of factor levels.
Experimental error is variation not explained by the factors in the design.
Example: For a heating experiment, temperature setting and exposure time may be factors; measured strength or energy use may be responses.
2. Why design before running
Define the question and response before choosing the experiment.
Choose factor ranges and levels that are meaningful and safe.
Control or record nuisance variables that could confound the result.
Plan enough runs and replication to understand variability.
Randomisation can reduce systematic bias from run order or uncontrolled influences.
Changing several things without a plan makes it difficult to know which change caused the observed result.
3. Main effects and interactions
A main effect describes how a factor changes the response on average across the studied conditions.
An interaction occurs when the effect of one factor depends on the level of another factor.
A design should be selected to estimate the effects relevant to the research question.
Interpret conclusions within the tested factor ranges.
If heating time helps only at a high temperature but not at a low temperature, time and temperature may interact.
4. Analyse and report
Record the exact settings, run order, measurements and deviations.
Compare responses using a method appropriate to the design and data.
Consider variability and uncertainty, not just the largest observed value.
Report limitations and avoid claims beyond what the experiment can establish.
DOE is not simply “do many experiments”; it is deliberate planning that makes experiments informative.
5. Experimental design vocabulary
A factor is an input or condition deliberately varied; a response is the outcome measured.
Randomization helps protect against systematic bias from uncontrolled or hidden influences; replication helps estimate experimental variability.
Factorial designs investigate combinations of factor levels, while incomplete designs may omit part of the comparison structure.
Example: vary temperature and concentration as factors and measure yield as the response.
6. Data summaries and response surfaces
Mean is the arithmetic average; median is the middle ordered value; mode is the most frequent value. These summaries and standard deviation retain the units of the measured quantity.
A probability density function describes a continuous random variable’s distribution; probability over an interval is represented by the area under its density.
In canonical response-surface analysis, curvature is examined through eigenvalues; a local maximum corresponds to negative curvature in every principal direction.
Calculation check: for {1, −1, −1, 1, 1, −1}, the sum is zero, so the mean is zero.
key: Factors are inputs; responses are measured outcomes.
Design is chosen to answer a question efficiently and reliably.
Randomisation, replication and control address different sources of uncertainty.
Interactions mean the effect of one factor may depend on another.
Experimental design vocabulary
Data summaries and response surfaces

8.overview: The textbook’s Week 8 is organised around department-specific research discussions and conversations with research scholars. Its contents span a wide range of disciplines. The key lesson is that research questions, methods, evidence and standards depend partly on the problem and field, while critical reasoning and responsible reporting remain broadly important.
sections: 1. Research differs across disciplines
Some fields rely heavily on controlled experiments; others use field observations, modelling, archival material, interviews or theoretical analysis.
A method should fit the question and the kind of evidence available.
Definitions of quality and suitable evidence may differ across fields.
Cross-disciplinary work requires careful explanation of terms and assumptions.
For example, a physical measurement study and a humanities interpretation need different evidence strategies, but both need a clear question and a defensible argument.
2. Learn from research scholars
Understand how a broad interest becomes a focused research question.
Ask how researchers choose methods and handle failed approaches.
Notice how they communicate limitations and make decisions under uncertainty.
Research paths often involve revision, collaboration and persistence.
A useful reflection after a research talk: What was the question? Why this method? What evidence changed the researcher’s thinking?
3. Build a research mindset
Read outside your narrow topic when it helps clarify the problem.
Explain assumptions so people from another discipline can evaluate the reasoning.
Use evidence and transparent methods to support conclusions.
Treat disciplinary examples as illustrations, not universal templates.
The uploaded textbook lists discussions from applied mechanics, engineering, humanities/social sciences, management, materials, mathematics, physics and other areas.
3. Research design and dissertation structure
Start by framing a research question; the question guides the design, the evidence to collect and the analysis that can answer it.
A dissertation commonly includes an introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion and conclusions, with references and other required front/back matter.
Validity, reliability and objectivity are related but distinct quality considerations; stronger research objectives should be clear and appropriate to the inquiry.
Study prompt: outline how a research question leads to a method, evidence, analysis and a defensible conclusion.
4. Interdisciplinary and participatory perspectives
Interdisciplinary research combines knowledge or methods from more than one discipline to address a problem that may not fit neatly inside one field.
Participatory research treats people and communities as contributors to inquiry; it is not merely knowledge production detached from participants.
Reference tools should match the information need: encyclopedias provide broad descriptive overviews, while bibliographies and directories serve different purposes.
Example: an environmental problem may require engineering measurements, biological interpretation and social context.
key: Methods must fit the research question and field.
Interdisciplinary research requires clear definitions and explicit assumptions.
Researcher experience can reveal iteration, uncertainty and method choice.
A single discipline’s method is not a universal template.
Research design and dissertation structure
Interdisciplinary and participatory perspectives

9.overview: The official course outline lists “Role of AI in Research” and “Research Journey” material in Week 9. Your textbook does not contain a confirmed detailed Week 9 chapter, so the notes here are a guided orientation to the listed topics, not a transcript reconstruction.
sections: 1. AI as a research aid
AI tools may help brainstorm search terms, organise notes, explain unfamiliar concepts or assist with coding and analysis.
The usefulness of a tool depends on the task, input quality and verification.
Generated summaries may omit nuance or misrepresent the source.
Researchers remain responsible for the claims and decisions in their work.
Use AI to generate possible search terms, then search the actual scholarly databases and read the primary sources.
2. Verify AI-assisted work
Check each important factual claim against a credible original source.
Open and confirm references rather than trusting a generated citation.
Do not upload confidential, personal or restricted material without permission.
Follow course, institution, publisher and funder rules for disclosure.
A citation that looks plausible is not proof that the cited paper exists or supports the claim.
3. Research journey
Research is iterative: questions, methods and interpretation can change as evidence accumulates.
Keep records of decisions, failed attempts and revised hypotheses.
Seek feedback and use it to improve the work.
These are general study principles; use the enrolled course’s lecture and assignment wording where it is available.
4. Research wellbeing and emotional regulation
Research life can include uncertainty, setbacks and breakthroughs; emotional experiences and relationships can influence the overall research experience.
After difficult feedback, pause before responding. Naming the emotion, breathing slowly, journaling or temporarily stepping away can support a more considered response.
Sleep, physical activity, recreation, reflection and social support help sustain work over time; prolonged distress and isolation can affect health and relationships.
Practice: distinguish constructive reflection from suppressing emotion or reacting immediately while upset.
5. Turn comparison into learning
A peer’s success can become a source of curiosity: examine what methods, timing, feedback or choices may be informative without concluding that one person is inherently more capable.
Working longer hours is not always the best response to being stuck; changing the approach, asking for help and taking a restorative break may be more productive.
Sustainable research combines independent thinking with appropriate support from advisers, labmates, friends and family.
Self-check: propose one constructive next step after a setback that protects both research quality and wellbeing.

AI output needs source-level verification.
The researcher remains accountable for the final work.

10.overview: The official course outline lists incremental versus transformational research and technology, plus imagination in research. The following explanations are concise study scaffolding around those published topic labels; the detailed lecture transcript for this week was not present in the supplied textbook.
sections: 1. Incremental research
Incremental work extends, refines or improves an existing line of work.
It may improve performance, reliability, cost, efficiency or understanding within an established framework.
A modest change can still be useful if it addresses a real limitation.
Example: Improving the calibration procedure of an existing sensor may be incremental research.
2. Transformational research
Transformational work changes a framing, capability or direction more fundamentally.
It may introduce a new way to define the problem or make a previously impractical approach possible.
The label should be justified by the significance of the change, not used as marketing language.
Example: A new sensing principle that enables a fundamentally different kind of measurement could be transformational, depending on evidence and impact.
3. Imagination in research
Imagination helps researchers propose questions and possible explanations.
Ideas must still be evaluated through logic, evidence, feasibility and ethical practice.
Exploring multiple possible futures can expose assumptions in current approaches.
Keep creative possibility separate from demonstrated result: a promising idea is a hypothesis until tested.
4. Incremental and transformational change
Incremental research improves, extends or refines an existing method, explanation, product or capability.
Transformational research changes a fundamental framing, opens a new direction or enables a qualitatively different capability.
The distinction is about the nature and scale of change, not a guarantee that one type is more valuable or successful.
Example: a small efficiency improvement is incremental; a new approach that changes how a class of problems is solved may be transformational.
5. Imagination as a research tool
Imagination helps researchers generate possible explanations and explore alternative futures, but a creative idea still needs critical evaluation.
Use evidence and feasibility checks to distinguish a promising idea from an unsupported claim.
Good research alternates between divergent thinking (generating possibilities) and convergent thinking (testing and refining them).
Study prompt: list two alternative explanations for an observation, then identify evidence that could distinguish them.
key: Incremental research extends or improves an existing direction.
Transformational research changes a framing or capability more fundamentally.
Imagination generates possibilities; evidence evaluates them.

11.overview: The official outline lists the role of AI in research, an introduction to generative AI and experience-sharing sessions. Your uploaded assignment archive includes questions about misleading recommendations from false or misleading material and about creativity/functional fixedness. This week’s notes combine the official topic labels with careful review prompts; the detailed lecture wording should take priority if available.
sections: 1. Generative AI basics
Generative AI produces new content such as text, images, code or other outputs based on learned patterns.
A fluent answer may still contain errors, unsupported claims or invented details.
Outputs depend on prompts, context and the system’s limitations.
Treat generated content as a draft or aid, not automatically as a verified source.
For a factual answer, independently confirm the claim and the source before relying on it.
2. Misleading source material
If training or supplied information contains false claims, a model may reproduce or amplify them.
A recommendation should be assessed by checking evidence and source quality, not by how confidently it is phrased.
Look for corroboration and distinguish the source’s claim from established evidence.
If a recommendation is based on a misleading article, trace the claim back to primary or reliable sources before acting.
3. Responsible research use
Protect sensitive data and respect privacy.
Check institutional policies and disclose AI assistance where required.
Verify generated references and quotations.
Retain human responsibility for interpretation, conclusions and decisions.
Do not present generated text as a primary source or claim to have performed work that was not performed.
4. Experience sharing
Reflect on how a researcher selected a question, learned from setbacks and chose a method.
Compare the reported experience with the course’s research principles.
Treat a personal example as a case, not as a universal rule.
Use the assignment screenshots for exact course-specific question wording.
5. LLM basics: tokens, context and parameters
Tokenization divides text into model-specific units such as word pieces; a token is not always the same as a whole word.
Context size is the amount of preceding input the model can attend to within its limit; parameters are learned numerical values in the model.
An LLM repeatedly predicts a next token conditioned on context to produce a sequence; sampling and decoding settings affect which token is selected.
Example: the same prompt with different context can produce different next-token probability distributions.
6. RAG, alignment and hallucinations
Retrieval-augmented generation adds relevant retrieved information to the model’s context; it does not inherently require retraining the entire model.
Alignment techniques aim to shape model behaviour toward desired outcomes, but they do not guarantee factual correctness.
Hallucinations are outputs that do not match ground truth; they are not necessarily deliberate lies. More context and verification can help but cannot guarantee elimination.
Safe workflow: verify important claims independently, inspect sources, and do not treat fluent language as proof.

3. Hypothesis development and falsifiability
A hypothesis is a testable, informed proposal that can be examined against observations; it should not be protected from every possible contradiction by untestable explanations.
Falsifiability asks whether some possible observation could show a claim to be false. A single black swan contradicts the universal claim that all swans are white.
Literature, observations and anomalies can reveal a missing link or contradiction from which a research question and hypothesis can develop.
Example: define what observation would count against a proposed relationship before collecting data.
4. Bloom’s taxonomy and creative thinking
Revised Bloom’s Taxonomy is commonly listed as Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate and Create.
Analyze, Evaluate and Create are the higher-order levels; PhD research may use multiple levels while moving from data to interpretation and new ideas.
Functional fixedness is a tendency to see an object only in its familiar use. Creativity can be practiced, and existing knowledge alone does not guarantee a novel contribution.
Self-check: map collecting data to relevant thinking levels, comparing hypotheses to evaluation, and generating a new research idea to creation.
